transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Since I stopped working full-time, I keep starting projects for the museum and then just never finishing them, even when I really want to. I retired from my handyman job about two years ago to do this volunteer work, but I'm really struggling to get things across the finish line.
Have you had similar problems with attention, organization, or finishing tasks since childhood or your school years, or did this only start after retirement?

Actually, these issues go all the way back to elementary school, where teachers always told my parents I was bright but constantly daydreaming, losing track of instructions, and forgetting to hand in homework. It has always been there in the background, but it really came to a head over the last couple of years since I retired and started trying to organize these volunteer projects.
Do you also have a long history of being restless, fidgety, or acting impulsively, or is the main problem just inattention and difficulty finishing tasks?

No, I’ve never really been restless, fidgety, or impulsive—the main issue has always been zoning out and struggling to finish tasks. Even back in elementary school, the feedback was always about me daydreaming and forgetting homework, rather than being hyperactive or disruptive. It's definitely just the inattention that gets in my way.
Do these attention problems also happen in more than one setting, such as at home, with hobbies, or in social situations, and do they regularly interfere with your daily life?

Yes, they definitely happen at home too; I'm constantly losing my reading glasses and notebook, and my wife often has to repeat herself because I zone out while looking right at her. It really interferes with my life because I've double-booked rooms and missed deadlines at the museum, which makes me feel unreliable and hesitant to take on new responsibilities.

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview confirms a lifelong pattern of inattention beginning in elementary school, with daydreaming, losing track of instructions, forgetting homework, losing items, difficulty finishing tasks, and impairment across multiple settings (home and volunteer work). Hyperactivity/impulsivity is denied. This is most consistent with an attention-deficit presentation; among the provided options, F98.8 is the only applicable code, though the history is also strongly suggestive of ADHD predominantly inattentive presentation.
